prayer.text: Our Lady of Beauraing and Banneux, pray for us.

cues.text: Five Children by a Railway Bridge
On the evening of November 29, 1932, in the small Belgian town of Beauraing, five children from two neighboring families were walking to fetch a schoolmate.
The children — the Voisins and the Degeimbres, ranging from nine to fifteen years old — saw a glowing white figure moving above a railway viaduct near a grotto dedicated to Our Lady of Lourdes.

Dismissed at first by their own skeptical parents, the children returned with the same account night after night until, over the following weeks, the apparitions became impossible for the village simply to ignore.
Beauraing in the early 1930s was a modest town of some two thousand residents.
The apparitions drew sudden, sustained attention, including vast numbers of pilgrims in the following year.
This transformed the community almost overnight from an obscure railway stop into a national point of pilgrimage.
The Golden Heart
Across thirty-three appearances between November 1932 and January 1933, the Lady gradually identified herself to the children as "the Immaculate Virgin."
In her final visits, she revealed a heart of gold radiating light upon her breast.
Devotion to Our Lady of the Golden Heart takes its name from this heart.
In her last apparition, on January 3, 1933, she directly asked the eldest child, Fernande, whether she loved her Son and herself.
Upon receiving the girl's yes, she instructed her simply, "Then sacrifice yourself for me," before bidding the children a final goodbye.
A Cautious, Sixteen-Year Inquiry

Belgian church authorities responded to the reports with considerable caution, forbidding public devotion at first and opening an investigation that would stretch on for sixteen years, during which the children's testimony was subjected to sustained and searching scrutiny.
Bishop André-Marie Charue of Namur authorized limited public devotion in 1943.
On July 2, 1949, he gave the apparitions final ecclesiastical approval.
They are among the most thoroughly vetted Marian apparitions the modern Church has examined.
Investigators paid particular attention to the consistency of the children's testimony across dozens of separate interviews conducted during the sixteen-year inquiry.
They carefully weighed whether five young witnesses from two ordinary working families could have sustained a fabricated account across so long and demanding a period of scrutiny.
A Poor Girl in a Neighboring Village
Barely fifty miles away, in the hamlet of Banneux, an eleven-year-old girl named Mariette Beco reported her own first vision on January 15, 1933.
She was the eldest of seven children in a struggling, not especially devout family, and this occurred only weeks after the Beauraing apparitions had concluded.
Looking out her kitchen window one January evening, Mariette saw a smiling young woman glowing softly in the family's garden.
Over eight appearances through early March, the Lady led her repeatedly to a small spring at the edge of the property.
"The Virgin of the Poor"
When Mariette finally asked who she was, the Lady answered simply, "I am the Virgin of the Poor."
She told her the nearby spring was reserved not for the girl alone but "for all nations, to relieve the sick."
Her recorded messages to Mariette across the eight visits amounted to barely ninety words in total—spare, tender, and entirely without embellishment.
On one occasion, she said: "I come to relieve suffering.
Believe in me, and I will believe in you."
Legacy
Bishop Louis-Joseph Kerkhofs of Liège formally approved the Banneux apparitions on August 22, 1949, just weeks after Beauraing received its own final approval.
Twin Belgian shrines were recognized within the same year, each centered on children of humble circumstance.
They were chosen, it seemed, precisely because they had nothing to offer beyond an open and trusting heart.

Both shrines remain active pilgrimage sites today, Beauraing known for its golden-hearted call to prayer and sacrifice, Banneux for its healing spring and its plain, unforgettable identification of Mary with the poor she came to console.
Some later commentators have noted that Beauraing and Banneux, arriving within weeks in neighboring corners of the same small country, seemed together to prepare Belgium.

This was for the darker trial of invasion and occupation that lay only a few years ahead, though the Church's own approved teaching on both apparitions rests on their content rather than on any such broader historical reading.
